histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.question: The hypodermis consists mainly of:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.explanation: The hypodermis (subcutis) is mainly adipose tissue providing insulation and cushioning.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.question: The commonest skin cancer, arising from basal keratinocytes, is:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.explanation: Basal cell carcinoma is the commonest skin cancer; it has a pearly rolled edge and rarely metastasises.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.question: Keratin pearls are a histological feature of:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.explanation: Keratin pearls (concentric keratinising whorls) are characteristic of squamous cell carcinoma.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.question: The prognosis of melanoma is best assessed by:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.explanation: Breslow thickness (depth of tumour invasion) is the key prognostic factor in melanoma.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.question: Psoriasis characteristically shows:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.explanation: Psoriasis shows parakeratosis, acanthosis, elongated rete ridges and neutrophilic Munro microabscesses.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.question: Pemphigus vulgaris causes blistering by:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.explanation: Pemphigus vulgaris is intra-epidermal blistering from anti-desmoglein (desmosome) antibodies; pemphigoid is subepidermal (hemidesmosome).

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.question: Spongiosis (intercellular epidermal oedema) is typical of:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.explanation: Spongiosis — intercellular oedema of the epidermis — is characteristic of eczema/dermatitis.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.question: Bullous pemphigoid produces a subepidermal blister by splitting at the:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.explanation: Bullous pemphigoid antibodies target hemidesmosomal BP180/BP230, splitting the skin through the lamina lucida (subepidermal); pemphigus splits at the desmosome (intra-epidermal).

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.question: Pemphigus vulgaris is caused by autoantibodies against:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.explanation: Pemphigus vulgaris antibodies target desmoglein 3 (± desmoglein 1), disrupting desmosomes to give a suprabasal intra-epidermal split ("row of tombstones").

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.question: In the epidermis, UVB converts 7-dehydrocholesterol to:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.explanation: UVB converts 7-dehydrocholesterol to cholecalciferol (D3) in the skin; the liver then 25-hydroxylates and the kidney 1α-hydroxylates it to active calcitriol.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.question: Which immunostain most specifically labels melanocytes and melanoma?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.explanation: Melanocytic lesions are SOX10/S100/Melan-A/HMB-45 positive; CK20 marks Merkel cells, CD1a marks Langerhans cells.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.question: The recognised in-situ precursor of invasive squamous cell carcinoma is:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.explanation: Bowen's disease is SCC in situ (full-thickness dysplasia, intact basement membrane); actinic keratosis is the earlier dysplastic precursor.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.question: The type VII collagen anchoring fibrils of the dermo-epidermal junction are defective in:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.explanation: Dystrophic epidermolysis bullosa results from type VII collagen (anchoring fibril) defects, splitting below the lamina densa.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.question: In albinism, the melanocytes are:
options: Present in normal number but unable to synthesise melanin
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Skin (.explanation: In albinism melanocytes are present in normal number and structure but cannot make melanin (e.g. tyrosinase deficiency); vitiligo, by contrast, destroys melanocytes.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.question: The pilosebaceous unit consists of:
options: Hair follicle + sebaceous gland + arrector pili muscle
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.explanation: The pilosebaceous unit is the hair follicle, its sebaceous gland and the arrector pili muscle.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.question: The inductive, vascular core at the base of the hair bulb is the:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.explanation: The dermal papilla is the vascular connective-tissue core that induces hair growth; the matrix around it proliferates.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.question: The cells that produce the hair shaft are in the:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.explanation: The matrix (around the dermal papilla) is the proliferating zone that produces the hair shaft.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.question: The layers of the hair shaft from inside out are:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.explanation: From inside out the hair shaft is medulla → cortex → cuticle.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.question: Hair colour is determined by melanocytes located in the:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.explanation: Melanocytes in the matrix add pigment to the growing hair; their decline causes greying.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.question: The active growth phase of the hair cycle is:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.explanation: Anagen is the active growth phase (lasting years); catagen is regression and telogen is rest/shedding.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.question: Hair follicle stem cells reside in the:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.explanation: Follicular stem cells lie in the bulge at the isthmus, near the arrector pili insertion.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.question: Sebaceous glands secrete by which mechanism?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.explanation: Sebaceous glands are holocrine — the entire lipid-laden cell disintegrates to release sebum.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.question: Sebaceous glands normally empty into the:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.explanation: Most sebaceous glands empty into the hair follicle via the pilosebaceous canal.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.question: Sebaceous gland activity is stimulated by:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.explanation: Androgens stimulate sebaceous glands, which is why sebum production increases at puberty.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.question: The arrector pili muscle is:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.explanation: The arrector pili is smooth muscle innervated by the sympathetic system; it raises the hair and expresses sebum.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.question: Which skin lacks hair follicles and sebaceous glands?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.explanation: Glabrous skin of the palms and soles has no hair follicles.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.question: Acne vulgaris involves all of the following EXCEPT:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.explanation: Acne results from follicular plugging, excess sebum, C. acnes and inflammation — not melanocyte destruction.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.question: Androgenetic alopecia is caused by follicle miniaturisation driven by:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.explanation: DHT drives progressive follicle miniaturisation in androgenetic alopecia; finasteride blocks its formation.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.question: Diffuse hair shedding after childbirth or severe illness is:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.explanation: A stressor synchronises many follicles into telogen, causing reversible diffuse shedding (telogen effluvium).

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.question: A blocked Meibomian gland of the eyelid produces a:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.explanation: A chalazion is a blocked/inflamed Meibomian (tarsal) sebaceous gland of the eyelid.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.question: Which is an example of a sebaceous gland opening directly onto the surface?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.explanation: Meibomian glands (and Montgomery glands of the areola) are sebaceous glands opening directly onto the surface.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.question: The 'holocrine' mode of secretion means:
options: The whole cell disintegrates to release its product
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.explanation: In holocrine secretion the entire cell breaks down to form the secretion (as in sebaceous glands).

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.question: Alopecia areata is best described as:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.explanation: Alopecia areata is autoimmune, non-scarring patchy hair loss with exclamation-mark hairs.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.question: Multiple sebaceous neoplasms can be a marker of which syndrome?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.explanation: Sebaceous tumours can indicate Muir–Torre syndrome, a variant of Lynch syndrome (mismatch-repair defect).

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.question: The inner root sheath layers from outside in are:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.explanation: The inner root sheath has three layers from outside in: Henle → Huxley → IRS cuticle; the IRS cuticle interlocks with the hair-shaft cuticle.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.question: The granule that keratinises the inner root sheath (analogous to keratohyalin) is:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.explanation: Trichohyalin granules keratinise the inner root sheath, the follicular analogue of keratohyalin in the epidermis.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.question: On the normal scalp, approximately what proportion of hairs are in anagen at any time?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.explanation: About 85–90% of scalp follicles are in anagen at any moment, ~1% in catagen and ~10–15% in telogen.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.question: The active shedding phase of the hair cycle, releasing the club hair, is:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.explanation: Exogen is the active shedding phase; telogen is the preceding resting phase and kenogen the empty-follicle interval.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.question: Scarring (cicatricial) alopecia is characterised by:
options: Destruction of the bulge with permanent loss of ostia
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.explanation: Scarring alopecia destroys the bulge stem-cell reservoir and follicular ostia, giving permanent hair loss (e.g. lichen planopilaris, discoid lupus).

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.question: Finasteride treats androgenetic alopecia by inhibiting:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.explanation: Finasteride inhibits 5-alpha-reductase, reducing conversion of testosterone to the follicle-miniaturising DHT.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.question: Which drug for severe acne is a potent teratogen requiring a pregnancy-prevention programme?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.explanation: Isotretinoin is a category-X retinoid teratogen; it requires contraception, monthly pregnancy tests and LFT/lipid monitoring.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.question: A recurrent, unilateral eyelid "chalazion" that fails to resolve should raise suspicion of:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Hair F.explanation: Sebaceous carcinoma of the Meibomian gland can masquerade as a recurrent chalazion/blepharitis and must be biopsied; it may signal Muir–Torre.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.question: Eccrine sweat glands open:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.explanation: Eccrine glands open directly onto the skin surface via a pore; apocrine glands open into hair follicles.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.question: The main function of eccrine sweat glands is:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.explanation: Eccrine glands produce watery sweat for evaporative cooling (thermoregulation).

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.question: Which cells of the eccrine secretory coil produce the watery component of sweat?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.explanation: Clear cells secrete the watery fluid (water and electrolytes); dark cells secrete glycoprotein.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.question: The eccrine sweat duct modifies the primary secretion by:
options: Reabsorbing Na+ and Cl- to make sweat hypotonic
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.explanation: The duct reabsorbs NaCl faster than water, producing hypotonic sweat.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.question: Eccrine sweat glands are controlled by:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.explanation: Uniquely, eccrine glands are innervated by sympathetic cholinergic (ACh) fibres.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.question: Apocrine sweat glands are found in the:
options: Axilla, groin, areola and external ear
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.explanation: Apocrine glands are restricted to the axilla, groin, areola, external ear and eyelid.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.question: Apocrine sweat glands open into the:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.explanation: Apocrine glands empty into the hair follicle, not directly onto the surface.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.question: Apocrine glands become functionally active:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.explanation: Apocrine glands develop and become active at puberty under androgen influence.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.question: Body odour from apocrine sweat is due to:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.explanation: Apocrine secretion is odourless until skin bacteria metabolise it, producing body odour.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.question: Ceruminous glands (which produce earwax) are modified:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.explanation: Ceruminous glands of the ear canal are modified apocrine glands.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.question: In cystic fibrosis, sweat chloride is high because:
options: Defective CFTR prevents chloride reabsorption in the duct
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.explanation: CFTR dysfunction prevents duct reabsorption of chloride, so sweat chloride is elevated (basis of the sweat test).

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.question: Botulinum toxin reduces sweating in hyperhidrosis by:
options: Blocking acetylcholine release at cholinergic nerve endings
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.explanation: Botulinum toxin blocks ACh release at the cholinergic fibres supplying eccrine glands, reducing sweating.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.question: Hidradenitis suppurativa is a disease of which glands?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.explanation: Hidradenitis suppurativa is chronic inflammation of apocrine-gland-bearing skin (axillae/groin).

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.question: Miliaria ('heat rash') is caused by:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.explanation: Miliaria results from obstruction of eccrine sweat ducts, trapping sweat and causing a vesicular rash.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.question: Which secretion mechanism do eccrine glands use?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.explanation: Eccrine glands secrete by the merocrine mode (exocytosis) with no loss of cytoplasm.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.question: The secretory coil differs from the duct histologically in that it is:
options: Larger and paler with myoepithelial cells
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.explanation: The secretory coil is larger, paler and has peripheral myoepithelial cells; the duct is smaller, darker and two-layered.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.question: Which gland type is the true thermoregulator?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.explanation: Eccrine glands provide thermoregulatory sweating; apocrine glands are scent-related.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.question: Compared with eccrine glands, apocrine glands are controlled by:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.explanation: Apocrine glands are sympathetic adrenergic; eccrine glands are sympathetic cholinergic.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.question: Absent or reduced sweat glands causing heat intolerance is seen in:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.explanation: Ectodermal dysplasia can feature reduced/absent sweat glands, causing anhidrosis and heat intolerance.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.question: Which statement correctly pairs a gland with its opening?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.explanation: Apocrine glands open into the hair follicle, whereas eccrine glands open onto the skin surface.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.question: Despite its name, the human axillary apocrine sweat gland secretes mainly by:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.explanation: Human "apocrine" sweat glands actually secrete largely by merocrine exocytosis; the name is a historical/ultrastructural misnomer.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.question: The true example of apocrine (decapitation) secretion is the:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.explanation: The lactating mammary gland is the classic decapitation-apocrine gland, releasing membrane-bound apical lipid droplets.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.question: The primary secretion produced by the eccrine secretory coil is:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.explanation: Clear cells make an isotonic, plasma-like primary secretion; the duct then reabsorbs NaCl to make the final sweat hypotonic.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.question: In the normal eccrine duct, chloride is reabsorbed through:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.explanation: CFTR reabsorbs Cl⁻ from the duct lumen (Na⁺ via ENaC); loss of CFTR in cystic fibrosis raises sweat chloride.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.question: The diagnostic sweat chloride threshold for cystic fibrosis (pilocarpine iontophoresis) is about:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.explanation: Sweat chloride ≥60 mmol/L is diagnostic of CF; 30–59 mmol/L is intermediate and <30 mmol/L normal.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.question: Gustatory facial sweating after parotid surgery (auriculotemporal nerve) is called:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.explanation: Frey syndrome is gustatory sweating from misdirected parasympathetic auriculotemporal fibres reinnervating cutaneous sweat glands.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.question: The constitutively secreted antimicrobial peptide of eccrine sweat is:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.explanation: Dermcidin is an eccrine-specific, constitutively secreted antimicrobial peptide contributing to skin innate immunity.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.question: Which benign eccrine sweat gland tumour presents as small periorbital papules?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Sweat.explanation: Syringoma is a benign eccrine ductal tumour typically seen as small papules around the eyes; cylindroma is the scalp "turban tumour".

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Eye (r.question: The layers of the cornea from anterior to posterior are:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Eye (r.explanation: Anterior to posterior: epithelium → Bowman's layer → stroma → Descemet's membrane → endothelium.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Eye (r.question: Corneal transparency depends on:
options: Regular collagen arrangement in the stroma and the endothelial water pump
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Eye (r.explanation: Regular stromal collagen spacing plus the endothelial pump keep the cornea dehydrated and transparent.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Eye (r.question: The corneal endothelium is important because it:
options: Pumps water out of the stroma to keep the cornea clear
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Eye (r.explanation: The endothelium pumps water out of the stroma; it does not regenerate, so its loss causes corneal oedema.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Eye (r.question: The cornea receives its oxygen mainly from:
options: The tear film (atmospheric oxygen) and aqueous humour
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Eye (r.explanation: Being avascular, the cornea is oxygenated by the tear film and aqueous humour (and nourished at the limbus).

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Eye (r.question: In the retina, the correct signal pathway is:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Eye (r.explanation: Light signals pass photoreceptor → bipolar cell → ganglion cell → optic nerve.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Eye (r.question: Which photoreceptors mediate colour and high-acuity vision, and where are they concentrated?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Eye (r.explanation: Cones mediate colour and acuity and are concentrated at the fovea; rods mediate dim/night vision peripherally.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Eye (r.question: The retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) does all of the following EXCEPT:
options: Transmit action potentials to the brain
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Eye (r.explanation: The RPE supports photoreceptors (phagocytosis, vitamin A, barrier, light absorption) but does not conduct impulses.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Eye (r.question: The fovea is characterised by:
options: Cones only and the highest visual acuity
A rich capillary network over the photoreceptors
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Eye (r.explanation: The fovea contains only cones and gives the highest acuity; it is an avascular pit.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Eye (r.question: The blind spot of the eye corresponds to the:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Eye (r.explanation: The optic disc, where axons exit and vessels enter, has no photoreceptors and forms the blind spot.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Eye (r.question: Rods contain which photopigment and mediate which vision?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Eye (r.explanation: Rods use rhodopsin (which requires vitamin A) for dim/night vision.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Eye (r.question: Lens fibres achieve transparency by:
options: Losing organelles and packing with crystallins
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Eye (r.explanation: Mature lens fibres lose their nuclei/organelles and are filled with regularly arranged crystallin proteins.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Eye (r.question: During accommodation for near vision, the ciliary muscle contracts and:
options: Zonules tighten and the lens flattens
Zonules relax and the lens becomes more rounded
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Eye (r.explanation: Ciliary muscle contraction relaxes the zonules, letting the elastic lens round up to increase refractive power.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Eye (r.question: Aqueous humour is produced by the ______ and drains via the ______.
options: ciliary body; trabecular meshwork and canal of Schlemm
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Eye (r.explanation: The ciliary body secretes aqueous, which drains through the trabecular meshwork into the canal of Schlemm.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Eye (r.question: Glaucoma is characterised by:
options: Raised intraocular pressure with optic-nerve damage and disc cupping
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Eye (r.explanation: Impaired aqueous drainage raises IOP, damaging the optic nerve and cupping the disc.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Eye (r.question: A painless progressive opacification of the lens is:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Eye (r.explanation: Cataract is opacification of the lens crystallins, causing painless progressive visual loss.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Eye (r.question: Drusen and RPE/photoreceptor damage at the macula characterise:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Eye (r.explanation: Age-related macular degeneration features drusen and RPE/photoreceptor damage, causing central vision loss.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Eye (r.question: Retinal detachment is separation of the:
options: Neural retina from the retinal pigment epithelium
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Eye (r.explanation: Retinal detachment is separation of the neural retina from the underlying RPE, causing field loss.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Eye (r.question: Fuchs' endothelial dystrophy affects which corneal layer, causing what?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Eye (r.explanation: Loss of corneal endothelial cells in Fuchs' dystrophy impairs the water pump, causing corneal oedema.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Eye (r.question: Retinitis pigmentosa is a progressive degeneration primarily of:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Eye (r.explanation: Retinitis pigmentosa is progressive rod degeneration, causing night blindness and tunnel vision.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Eye (r.question: The histological hallmark of retinoblastoma is:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Eye (r.explanation: Retinoblastoma shows Flexner–Wintersteiner rosettes and is linked to RB1 gene mutation.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Eye (r.question: In the dark, retinal photoreceptors are:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Eye (r.explanation: The "dark current" keeps cGMP-gated channels open, so photoreceptors are depolarised and tonically release glutamate; light hyperpolarises them.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Eye (r.question: Light striking rhodopsin isomerises:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Eye (r.explanation: Photon absorption isomerises 11-cis retinal to all-trans retinal, activating the transducin/PDE cascade that lowers cGMP and closes cation channels.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Eye (r.question: The inner blood-retinal barrier is formed by:
options: Tight junctions of the retinal capillary endothelium
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Eye (r.explanation: The inner BRB is the tight junctions of non-fenestrated retinal capillary endothelium; the outer BRB is RPE tight junctions.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Eye (r.question: The neural retina and the RPE both develop from:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Eye (r.explanation: The two walls of the optic cup (neuroectoderm) form the neural retina and the RPE; their potential space is where retinal detachment occurs.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Eye (r.question: An acute painful red eye with a fixed mid-dilated pupil and haloes around lights suggests:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Eye (r.explanation: Acute angle-closure glaucoma is an emergency: sudden angle blockage causes a painful red eye, cloudy cornea and a fixed mid-dilated pupil.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Eye (r.question: Wet (neovascular) age-related macular degeneration is treated with:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Eye (r.explanation: Choroidal neovascularisation in wet AMD is treated with intravitreal anti-VEGF (e.g. ranibizumab, aflibercept).

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Eye (r.question: The lateral interneurons of the outer plexiform layer are the:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Eye (r.explanation: Horizontal cells mediate lateral interactions in the outer plexiform layer; amacrine cells do so in the inner plexiform layer.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Eye (r.question: Aqueous humour is actively secreted by the ______, in a process dependent on ______.
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Eye (r.explanation: The non-pigmented ciliary epithelium secretes aqueous via carbonic anhydrase (hence acetazolamide/dorzolamide lower intraocular pressure).

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Eye (r.question: A cherry-red spot at the macula with sudden painless monocular visual loss indicates:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Eye (r.explanation: CRAO gives a pale ischaemic retina with a cherry-red foveal spot and sudden painless monocular loss — a retinal emergency.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Ear (c.question: The organ of Corti is located on the:
options: Basilar membrane in the scala media
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Ear (c.explanation: The organ of Corti (the hearing sensory organ) sits on the basilar membrane within the scala media.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Ear (c.question: The main afferent (sensory) cells of hearing are the:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Ear (c.explanation: Inner hair cells are the primary sensory cells; outer hair cells amplify basilar-membrane motion.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Ear (c.question: Sound transduction occurs when hair-cell stereocilia bend against the:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Ear (c.explanation: Basilar-membrane vibration bends the stereocilia against the tectorial membrane, depolarising the hair cells.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Ear (c.question: The endolymph of the scala media is characteristically high in:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Ear (c.explanation: Endolymph is high in K+ (produced by the stria vascularis); perilymph is high in Na+.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Ear (c.question: Endolymph is secreted by the:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Ear (c.explanation: The stria vascularis in the cochlear duct wall produces the K+-rich endolymph.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Ear (c.question: According to cochlear tonotopy, high frequencies are detected at the:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Ear (c.explanation: The stiff narrow base detects high frequencies; the wide floppy apex detects low frequencies.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Ear (c.question: Which cranial nerve carries auditory and vestibular signals?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Ear (c.explanation: The vestibulocochlear nerve (CN VIII) carries hearing (cochlear) and balance (vestibular) signals.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Ear (c.question: The maculae of the utricle and saccule detect:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Ear (c.explanation: Maculae detect linear acceleration and gravity via otolith-weighted hair cells.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Ear (c.question: The cristae ampullares of the semicircular canals detect:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Ear (c.explanation: Cristae ampullares detect angular acceleration via hair cells projecting into the cupula.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Ear (c.question: Otoliths (otoconia) are found in the:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Ear (c.explanation: Otoliths sit on the otolithic membrane of the maculae, weighting them to respond to gravity/linear acceleration.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Ear (c.question: The pinna is composed of:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Ear (c.explanation: The pinna is elastic cartilage covered by skin.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Ear (c.question: Ceruminous glands of the ear canal are modified:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Ear (c.explanation: Ceruminous glands (earwax) are modified apocrine glands.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Ear (c.question: Which ossicle transmits vibration to the oval window?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Ear (c.explanation: The stapes footplate vibrates the oval window, transmitting sound into the inner-ear fluid.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Ear (c.question: The Eustachian tube functions to:
options: Equalise middle-ear pressure with the nasopharynx
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Ear (c.explanation: The Eustachian tube connects the middle ear to the nasopharynx and equalises pressure.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Ear (c.question: Otosclerosis causes conductive hearing loss by:
options: Fixation of the stapes footplate at the oval window
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Ear (c.explanation: Otosclerosis fixes the stapes at the oval window, impairing sound conduction.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Ear (c.question: Presbycusis and noise-induced hearing loss first affect:
options: High frequencies via outer hair cells at the base
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Ear (c.explanation: Outer hair cells at the cochlear base (high-frequency region) are lost first.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Ear (c.question: Ménière's disease is due to:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Ear (c.explanation: Ménière's disease is endolymphatic hydrops, causing episodic vertigo, tinnitus and fluctuating hearing loss.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Ear (c.question: Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV) is caused by:
options: Displaced otoliths entering a semicircular canal
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Ear (c.explanation: BPPV results from otoconia displaced into a semicircular canal, triggering brief positional vertigo.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Ear (c.question: A collection of keratinising squamous epithelium in the middle ear is a:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Ear (c.explanation: A cholesteatoma is keratinising squamous epithelium in the middle ear that can erode bone.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Ear (c.question: An acoustic neuroma is a:
options: Vestibular schwannoma at the cerebellopontine angle
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Ear (c.explanation: An acoustic neuroma is a vestibular schwannoma causing unilateral sensorineural hearing loss and tinnitus.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Ear (c.question: Hair-cell depolarisation during transduction is driven by the influx of:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Ear (c.explanation: Uniquely, K+ flows into the hair cell from the K+-rich endolymph through open MET channels, depolarising it (driven by the +80 mV endocochlear potential).

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Ear (c.question: The +80 mV endocochlear potential is generated by the:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Ear (c.explanation: The stria vascularis in the lateral wall of the cochlear duct maintains the K+-rich endolymph and the +80 mV endocochlear potential.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Ear (c.question: The motor protein responsible for outer hair cell electromotility is:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Ear (c.explanation: Prestin in the outer hair cell membrane produces electromotility (the cochlear amplifier), boosting basilar-membrane vibration and generating otoacoustic emissions.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Ear (c.question: Otoacoustic emissions used in newborn hearing screening are generated by the:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Ear (c.explanation: Otoacoustic emissions arise from outer hair cell electromotility; their absence suggests cochlear (outer hair cell) dysfunction.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Ear (c.question: The roof of the scala media (cochlear duct) is formed by:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Ear (c.explanation: Reissner's membrane roofs the scala media, separating its endolymph from the perilymph of the scala vestibuli.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Ear (c.question: In a patient with conductive hearing loss of the right ear, Weber's test lateralises:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Ear (c.explanation: Weber lateralises TO the affected ear in conductive loss (and AWAY from the affected ear in sensorineural loss).

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Ear (c.question: Bilateral vestibular schwannomas (acoustic neuromas) are pathognomonic of:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Ear (c.explanation: Bilateral vestibular schwannomas define neurofibromatosis type 2; MRI of the internal auditory meatus is the investigation of choice.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Ear (c.question: Which ototoxic agents typically cause REVERSIBLE hearing loss/tinnitus?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Ear (c.explanation: High-dose salicylates and quinine cause reversible tinnitus/SNHL; aminoglycosides and cisplatin cause irreversible cumulative damage.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Ear (c.question: The cell bodies of the afferent cochlear nerve neurons lie in the:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Ear (c.explanation: The bipolar afferent neurons have their cell bodies in the spiral ganglion within the modiolus; most synapse on inner hair cells.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Olfact.question: The olfactory epithelium is a specialised:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Olfact.explanation: The olfactory epithelium is a tall pseudostratified columnar epithelium.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Olfact.question: Which feature distinguishes olfactory from respiratory epithelium?
options: Absence of goblet cells with Bowman's glands and nerve bundles beneath
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Olfact.explanation: Olfactory epithelium lacks goblet cells and has Bowman's glands and olfactory nerve bundles in the lamina propria.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Olfact.question: The primary sensory cells of smell are the:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Olfact.explanation: Olfactory receptor (bipolar) neurons are the sensory transducers; their cilia bear the odorant receptors.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Olfact.question: Olfactory receptor neurons are unusual because they:
options: Are continuously replaced from basal cells throughout life
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Olfact.explanation: They regenerate from basal stem cells throughout life — a rare example of adult neurogenesis.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Olfact.question: The odorant receptors are located on the neuron's:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Olfact.explanation: Odorant receptors sit on the non-motile olfactory cilia projecting from the olfactory knob.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Olfact.question: Basal cells of the olfactory epithelium function as:
options: Stem cells regenerating neurons and sustentacular cells
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Olfact.explanation: Basal cells are the stem cells that regenerate receptor neurons and sustentacular cells.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Olfact.question: Bowman's glands secrete a serous fluid that:
options: Dissolves odorants and moistens the surface
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Olfact.explanation: Bowman's (olfactory) glands provide serous fluid in which odorants dissolve to reach the receptors.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Olfact.question: Olfactory nerve axons reach the olfactory bulb by passing through the:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Olfact.explanation: Olfactory axons pierce the cribriform plate of the ethmoid bone to reach the olfactory bulb.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Olfact.question: Which is TRUE of the central olfactory pathway?
options: It relays in the thalamus before any cortex
It reaches the primary (piriform) cortex without an obligatory thalamic relay
It crosses in the optic chiasm
It synapses in the cochlear nuclei
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Olfact.explanation: Olfaction reaches the primary (piriform) olfactory cortex without an obligatory thalamic relay; only conscious discrimination uses a mediodorsal-thalamus → orbitofrontal route.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Olfact.question: The output neurons of the olfactory bulb are the:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Olfact.explanation: Mitral cells are the olfactory bulb's output neurons, projecting via the olfactory tract.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Olfact.question: The olfactory cilia differ from respiratory cilia in being:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Olfact.explanation: Olfactory cilia are non-motile and carry odorant receptors, unlike the motile cilia of respiratory epithelium.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Olfact.question: Head trauma commonly causes anosmia by:
options: Shearing the olfactory nerves at the cribriform plate
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Olfact.explanation: A blow can shear the fine olfactory filaments where they cross the cribriform plate, causing anosmia.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Olfact.question: COVID-19 causes loss of smell mainly by infecting the:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Olfact.explanation: SARS-CoV-2 infects the sustentacular cells, disrupting olfactory function (usually reversibly).

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Olfact.question: Anosmia can be an early feature of:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Olfact.explanation: Anosmia often precedes the motor/cognitive features of Parkinson's and Alzheimer's disease.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Olfact.question: Kallmann syndrome combines anosmia with:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Olfact.explanation: Kallmann syndrome is anosmia plus hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, from failed GnRH/olfactory neuron migration.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Olfact.question: A malignant tumour arising from the olfactory epithelium is:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Olfact.explanation: Esthesioneuroblastoma (olfactory neuroblastoma) arises from the olfactory epithelium of the nasal roof.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Olfact.question: A cribriform-plate fracture may cause:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Olfact.explanation: Breaching the cribriform plate can allow CSF to leak into the nose, risking meningitis.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Olfact.question: Which cell supports and insulates the olfactory receptor neurons?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Olfact.explanation: Sustentacular (supporting) cells support and insulate the receptor neurons.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Olfact.question: The olfactory receptor neuron is best described as a:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Olfact.explanation: Olfactory receptor neurons are bipolar, with an apical dendrite (cilia) and a basal axon to CN I.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Olfact.question: Why is olfactory epithelium yellowish-brown grossly?
options: Lipofuscin pigment in sustentacular cells and glands
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Olfact.explanation: Lipofuscin pigment in the sustentacular cells and Bowman's glands gives the epithelium a yellow-brown colour.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Olfact.question: According to the "one neuron–one receptor" rule, each olfactory receptor neuron expresses:
options: A random new receptor each day
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Olfact.explanation: Each neuron expresses a single odorant-receptor gene; like-receptor axons converge on the same glomerulus, giving combinatorial odour coding.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Olfact.question: In olfactory transduction, cAMP opens a CNG cation channel and the depolarisation is then amplified by:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Olfact.explanation: Ca2+ entering through the CNG channel opens a Ca2+-activated Cl- channel; because intracellular Cl- is high, Cl- flows out and amplifies the depolarisation.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Olfact.question: The glia that ensheath olfactory axons and support their lifelong regrowth are:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Olfact.explanation: Olfactory ensheathing cells wrap the unmyelinated olfactory axons and guide their continuous regeneration into the CNS bulb.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Olfact.question: A distorted perception of a real smell (often during recovery) is termed:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Olfact.explanation: Parosmia is a distorted perception of an actual odorant, commonly seen as regenerating axons mis-wire during recovery.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Olfact.question: When testing the olfactory nerve, which agent should be AVOIDED because it stimulates the trigeminal nerve?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Olfact.explanation: Ammonia and pungent agents stimulate trigeminal (CN V) free nerve endings, so an anosmic patient still reacts — giving a false result.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Olfact.question: The olfactory tract projects directly (bypassing the thalamus) to a primary olfactory cortex that includes which structures?
options: The piriform cortex, amygdala and entorhinal cortex
The lateral geniculate nucleus and occipital cortex
The primary auditory cortex of the superior temporal gyrus
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Olfact.explanation: The olfactory tract projects directly to the primary olfactory (piriform) cortex, amygdala, entorhinal cortex and olfactory tubercle — the only sensory modality reaching cortex without an obligatory thalamic relay. The distractors are the cortices/relays for vision (LGN/occipital), hearing (superior temporal), touch (postcentral) and motor coordination (cerebellum), none of which receive direct olfactory input.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Olfact.question: The active, day-to-day progenitor cells of the olfactory epithelium are the:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Olfact.explanation: Globose basal cells are the active transit-amplifying progenitors; horizontal basal cells are the quiescent reserve stem cells.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Olfact.question: In Kallmann syndrome, MRI characteristically shows:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Olfact.explanation: Failure of olfactory bulb/GnRH-neuron development in Kallmann syndrome gives absent/hypoplastic olfactory bulbs on MRI with hypogonadotropic hypogonadism.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Taste.question: Taste buds are found on all of the following EXCEPT:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Taste.explanation: Filiform papillae are keratinised and lack taste buds; fungiform, circumvallate and foliate papillae bear them.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Taste.question: The most numerous papillae, which are keratinised and have no taste buds, are:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Taste.explanation: Filiform papillae are the most numerous, keratinised, and provide a rough surface but have no taste buds.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Taste.question: Circumvallate papillae are characterised by:
options: A V-shaped arrangement at the back, a surrounding moat, many taste buds and von Ebner's glands
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Taste.explanation: Circumvallate papillae sit in a V at the back of the tongue within a trench, with many taste buds flushed by von Ebner's glands.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Taste.question: Von Ebner's glands are:
options: Serous glands emptying into circumvallate trenches
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Taste.explanation: Von Ebner's serous glands empty into the circumvallate trenches, flushing tastants and secreting lingual lipase.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Taste.question: Taste cells that detect sweet, bitter and umami via GPCRs are:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Taste.explanation: Type II receptor cells detect sweet, bitter and umami through GPCRs (T1R/T2R).

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Taste.question: Which taste cell detects sour and forms a true synapse with the nerve?
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Taste.explanation: Type III (presynaptic) cells detect sour and synapse with the gustatory afferent.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Taste.question: Basal cells of the taste bud function as:
options: Stem cells that regenerate taste cells
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Taste.explanation: Basal cells are stem cells that continuously regenerate the taste cells (~10–14 day turnover).

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Taste.question: Salty and sour tastes are transduced respectively by:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Taste.explanation: Salt is sensed via Na+ channels and sour via H+ ions; sweet, bitter and umami use GPCRs.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Taste.question: Taste from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue is carried by:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Taste.explanation: The facial nerve (CN VII) via the chorda tympani carries taste from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Taste.question: Taste from the posterior third of the tongue is carried by:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Taste.explanation: The glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) carries taste from the posterior third of the tongue.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Taste.question: Taste from the epiglottis and pharynx is carried by:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Taste.explanation: The vagus nerve (CN X) carries taste from the epiglottis and pharynx.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Taste.question: All taste afferents first synapse in the:
options: Nucleus of the solitary tract (nucleus solitarius)
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Taste.explanation: Taste fibres converge on the nucleus solitarius, then relay to the thalamus and gustatory cortex.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Taste.question: Taste receptor cells are:
options: Specialised epithelial cells that are continually replaced
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Taste.explanation: Taste cells are modified epithelial cells that signal to sensory nerves and are renewed by basal cells.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Taste.question: The taste pore is:
options: The apical opening through which tastants reach the microvilli
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Taste.explanation: The taste pore is the apical opening of the taste bud through which dissolved tastants reach the sensory microvilli.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Taste.question: Why does anosmia reduce the perception of 'taste'?
options: Flavour is largely smell, so losing olfaction makes food seem bland
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Taste.explanation: Flavour combines taste and smell; without olfaction, food seems bland despite intact basic tastes.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Taste.question: A lesion of the facial nerve (e.g. Bell's palsy) can cause:
options: Loss of taste from the posterior third
Loss of taste from the anterior two-thirds (chorda tympani)
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Taste.explanation: The facial nerve's chorda tympani supplies taste to the anterior two-thirds of the tongue.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Taste.question: A common nutritional cause of impaired taste is:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Taste.explanation: Zinc deficiency is a recognised cause of ageusia/dysgeusia.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Taste.question: Geographic tongue is due to:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Taste.explanation: Geographic tongue is benign migratory loss of filiform papillae, giving map-like red patches.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Taste.question: Which statement about the 'tongue taste map' is correct?
options: Sweet is only tasted at the tip
Bitter is only at the sides
Sour is only at the back
It is a myth; all taste qualities are detectable across the tongue
Salt is only in the middle
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Taste.explanation: The regional tongue taste map is a myth; all basic tastes can be detected across the tongue surface.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Taste.question: Umami taste is typically triggered by:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Taste.explanation: Umami (savoury) taste is triggered by glutamate and sensed by type II cells via GPCRs.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Taste.question: Sour taste is transduced by protons acting through the:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Taste.explanation: OTOP1 is the proton channel in PKD2L1-expressing type III cells that transduces sour taste.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Taste.question: The taste-specific G-protein coupling sweet, bitter and umami receptors is:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Taste.explanation: Gustducin is the taste-specific G-protein coupling T1R/T2R receptors in type II cells to the transduction cascade.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Taste.question: Type II taste cells signal to the afferent nerve by releasing ATP through:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Taste.explanation: Type II cells lack classic synapses; they release ATP through the voltage-gated CALHM1/CALHM3 channel to excite the afferent.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Taste.question: Appetitive (low) salt taste is sensed via the amiloride-sensitive:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Taste.explanation: The epithelial sodium channel (ENaC) mediates appetitive salt taste and is blocked by amiloride.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Taste.question: The first-order sensory neurons for taste from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue lie in the:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Taste.explanation: The chorda tympani (CN VII) taste fibres have their cell bodies in the geniculate ganglion.

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Taste.question: Central taste information projects to the:
options: Ipsilateral VPM of the thalamus, then the gustatory cortex
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Taste.explanation: Taste is relayed ipsilaterally: NST → ipsilateral VPM thalamus → gustatory cortex (insula/frontal operculum).

histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Taste.question: The molecular marker of sour-sensing (type III) taste cells is:
histology__SKIN & SPECIAL SENSES__Taste.explanation: PKD2L1 marks the type III sour-sensing cells, which use the OTOP1 proton channel.
